claim: Both civil-war and world-war dynamics are going on today.
criterion: No observable criterion or date given.

claim: Comparing the present to the template, we are heading into one of the cases in which central governments and central banks 'go broke'.
criterion: 'Going broke' is defined (central bank must print to service its debt) but no date or threshold is attached; only partly testable.

claim: US government debt divided by US gold holdings is 37x and money supply divided by gold is 6x today, versus 7x and 1.3x in 1945.
criterion: Recompute the ratios with stated definitions of debt and money supply.

claim: We are likely entering the very turbulent stage of the Overall Big Cycle and changes in the world order will be big.
criterion: No criterion for 'turbulent' or 'big'.

claim: As of March 2025 there have been 12 complete US short-term debt cycles since 1945 and the US is about two-thirds through the 13th.
horizon: implies the 13th cycle ends around 2027 under the 6 ± 3 year rule
criterion: A recession/trough marking the end of the 13th cycle would be expected roughly 2 years after March 2025 (wide band given ±3 years).

claim: Holders of Japanese bonds have lost 45% relative to holding US dollar debt and 60% relative to gold since 2013.
criterion: Compute JGB total return versus USD debt and gold from 2013.

claim: US government expenditures excluding interest will average ~112% of income over the next decade (primary deficit ~12% of income) and the US borrows ~20% of its income each year to cover interest.
criterion: Compare realized primary deficit and interest as % of federal revenue with CBO's baseline.

claim: US government debt is ~580-583% of revenue and is projected to reach ~700% in 10 years if rates equal growth, ~650% using CBO's rate-growth gap; CBO's own projection is 648% of revenue (118% of GDP) in 2035.
criterion: Federal debt / federal revenue in 2035.

claim: CBO projects effective interest rates averaging 3.45% and nominal growth of 3.9% over the next decade, a gap of about −0.4%.
criterion: Realized average effective rate and nominal GDP growth 2025-2035.

claim: Extending the Trump tax cuts adds annual spending of 1.5% of GDP or 8% of government revenue (CBO).
criterion: CBO scoring of extension.

claim: About 35% of US government debt matures each year and M0 is about $5.7T, roughly 110% of government income.
criterion: Treasury maturity profile and monetary base data.

claim: If debt growth remains as projected, central banks will have to push real interest rates lower, making debt assets less attractive to lender-creditors.
criterion: Conditional: if debt/revenue tracks the projection, observe whether US real rates are pushed down (via buying) relative to today; 'have to' is a judgment but the direction is observable.

claim: To stabilize US debt-to-income over 10 years, one of: nominal rates fall to ~1%; inflation rises to ~4.5% (nominal growth ~6.5%); spending is cut 12% (47% of discretionary); or revenue rises 11%.
criterion: Arithmetic under CBO assumptions; recompute with Formula 1 and CBO inputs.

claim: Country ratios: USA debt 100% of GDP / 583% of revenue, deficit 6% of GDP / 37% of revenue, revenue 17% of GDP; JPN 215/1376/4/26/16; CHN 90/321/5/16/28 (incl. local governments); FRA 86/478/6/31/18; DEU 44/340/2/17/13; GBR 92/256/6/16/36.
criterion: Compare with IMF/national fiscal data for 2024-2025.

claim: Policy makers' belief that controlling out-year deficits will give investors confidence is naive because it ignores who will buy and sell the bonds.
criterion: Evaluative statement about reasoning, not an outcome.

claim: Over the last 20 years falling Japanese interest rates have made debt grow slowly and debt service shrink.
criterion: Japanese government interest cost and debt trajectory 2005-2025.

claim: US monetary regimes: MP0 1945-1971, MP1 1971-2008, MP2 2008-2020 (MP3 implied from 2020).
criterion: Definitional periodization; dates are checkable but the classification is his.

claim: Rating agencies do not rate the risk of government debt losing value through devaluation; Dalio rates central government and central bank debt separately and treats devaluation as at least as probable as default.
criterion: Methodological statement.

claim: Breakthroughs in AI put us on the brink of almost understanding the whole economic machine.
criterion: No criterion.

claim: Since the start of 2013 JGB holders have lost 60% vs gold, 45% vs US-dollar debt and 6% in domestic purchasing power (average inflation ~1%); gradual devaluation because the yen is fiat.
criterion: Recompute JGB returns vs gold, USD bonds and Japanese CPI from January 2013.

claim: Cutting the social safety net is a political third rail today in Brazil and the US.
criterion: Sustained enacted safety-net cuts would contradict it.

claim: The US, Europe, the UK and Japan post-financial-crisis are recent cases 'still playing out' within the archetypal sequence (excluded from ex-ongoing charts).
criterion: These economies exit without the Stage 3-7 dynamics (debt squeeze, net selling, devaluation/restructuring).

claim: The US government is not yet on the indefinitely rising debt and debt-service path seen at devaluation points, but it is moving toward it.
criterion: Projected US debt/GDP and interest/revenue keep rising; falsified if they stabilize or fall.

claim: Government interest service in Europe, Japan and China is around half that of the US as a share of GDP (Europe/China lower government debt; Japan much lower rates).
criterion: Compare government interest/GDP across the four.

claim: Japan's government debt of about 215% of GDP could become a problem if refinanced at higher rates.
criterion: Rising JGB refinancing rates lift interest/revenue materially.

claim: The doom-loop downward spiral in the value of government debt has not yet happened in the US, Europe, Japan or China.
criterion: A self-reinforcing government-bond sell-off forcing losses or devaluation in these markets.

claim: QE since 2008: US four waves = 18% of potential GDP, 5% of total debt, 16% of government debt; Europe four waves = 30%, 10%, 36%; Japan three waves = 95%, 22%, 46%.
criterion: Measure cumulative central-bank purchases vs potential GDP, total debt and government debt.

claim: Several central banks have negative net equity (or equivalent) today without much operational hindrance; this is a moderate red flag.
criterion: Central-bank balance sheets show negative equity; operations unimpaired.

claim: Turkey 'today' (Jan-23 to early 2024): central-bank balance sheet 17.2% of GDP, cash-flow losses -2.6% of GDP, net reserves -2.5% of GDP, money growth 20%, inflation 84%, cumulative FX move -42%, losses paid by money printing.
criterion: Check against CBRT and Turkish statistics for the period.

claim: Digital currencies like Bitcoin may benefit as real assets in the next government-debt devaluation ('perhaps this time').
criterion: Hedged; testable only at the next episode by comparing Bitcoin to local cash.

claim: We are 80 years into the Overall Big Cycle that began at the end of WWII (1945), unfolding in the classic way toward dramatic changes.
criterion: Monetary, internal and world orders undergo radical change within the remaining cycle horizon; persistence of the existing orders would contradict it.

claim: We are now in the late-cycle 'Stage 5' of the Overall Big Cycle, just before the depression-and-war stage that ends the Big Cycle.
criterion: The next major phase is a depression/war with revolutionary changes in monetary, internal and world orders.

claim: Existing circumstances: great overindebtedness in the US and all other major countries simultaneously; nationalistic, fragmented internal orders; contentious international relations; adverse, expensive acts of nature; amazing new technologies.
criterion: Each item is checkable against data on debt, polarization, conflict, disasters, technology.

claim: Past over-indebted countries (incl. the US) pressured others to buy their debt, froze/seized 'enemy' assets, restructured via maturity extension/monetization, imposed confiscatory taxes and capital/FX controls, revalued government assets and created new money - raised as possibilities, explicitly not predictions.
criterion: Not a forecast by his own framing; each action is observable if it occurs.

claim: The honeymoon-then-disappointment leader dynamic is at play in the US as of March 2025.
criterion: Support wanes and more extreme actions to hold power follow; sustained support without escalation would contradict it.

claim: Big political shifts toward autocracy, mostly toward the hard right, are now taking place for the same reasons as past transitions; such transfers usually become increasingly extreme over three to five years within the democracy's rules.
criterion: Increasingly extreme consolidation of power in affected democracies over the next few years.

claim: Multilateralism is fading into irrelevance and unilateralism is rising; multilateral organizations' power is declining rapidly and shifting to the major powers; 'the strong prey on the weak' is typical of our stage of the Big Cycle.
criterion: Declining institutional capacity (UN, WTO, etc.) and rising unilateral actions; a revival of effective multilateralism would contradict it.

claim: Droughts, floods and pandemics are increasing and increasingly costly and will almost certainly get worse; nearly all nations face debt issues, so there isn't enough money for climate mitigation/adaptation.
criterion: Disaster frequency/cost series keep rising; public climate spending stays below needs.

claim: AI advances will dramatically affect all thinking in all areas for good or bad; technology booms financed by unsustainable credit produce bubbles and busts.
criterion: The bubble clause is testable for the AI boom (credit-financed? followed by a bust?); the first clause is not.

claim: Dealing with problems together would give the best results but is probably still beyond humankind's capabilities because human nature hasn't changed.
criterion: Not testable.

claim: The US is in the leveraging-up phase of the long-term debt cycle and has not yet entered the deleveraging part; it is about two-thirds through its 13th post-1945 short-term debt cycle (12 completed, ~6 years each)
criterion: A simultaneous fall in US private and public debt/GDP (deleveraging), or the 13th cycle ending on a different timetable

claim: US central government debt/GDP is at its highest since 1946 and projected much higher (CBO dots ~120% in 10 years, ~140% in 20 years)
criterion: Realized federal debt/GDP vs the ~120%/~140% dots

claim: Central government debt service is about 100% of revenue and projected to rise to about 150% in 15 years
criterion: Debt service (principal+interest)/revenue path

claim: Commercial-bank and foreign holders of Treasuries have become sellers and are unlikely to buy at past scale, especially if the US mishandles debt/policy, threatens sanctions, returns are bad, or US prominence declines
criterion: Foreign official and bank share of Treasury holdings over time

claim: Fed mark-to-market loss of ~$700B (2.5% of GDP) is a red flag; a big selling of US debt would force either an intolerable rise in rates and a severe contraction or large printing and devaluation, and would call Fed independence into question
criterion: If a Treasury sell-off occurs: rate spike/contraction or renewed Fed buying; political challenge to Fed independence

claim: Debt burdens are projected to grow substantially across the developed world over coming decades (chart to 2050: World, G7, US, China, Japan, UK, France, Italy rising; Germany falling)
criterion: Government debt/GDP paths vs the Bloomberg Economics forecast lines

claim: Some countries are encountering the late stages of their Big Debt Cycles and will likely experience serious consequences
criterion: Vague; no named countries or dates

claim: We are near the end of the monetary, domestic and international orders that began in 1945 and of the current Big Cycle
criterion: Only ex post via emergence of a new monetary/geopolitical order

claim: Taiwan is the center of chip production, more important than oil was in the last cycle; Chinese leaders expect to eventually take control of Taiwan and parts of the South China Sea
criterion: Ex post: Chinese control of Taiwan / South China Sea features

claim: Investors who have only known positive real equity returns and invest only in equity-like assets are making a mistake
criterion: Judgment about investor behavior

claim: Trump-era shifts toward aggressive, nationalist, protectionist, militaristic policy are analogous to the periods before WWI and WWII; post-2008 developments are analogous to the early 1930s; post-2008 geopolitical resets are analogous to 1933-38
criterion: Analogy; only outcomes (war/no war) would bear on it

claim: Post-2021 tightening brought the real bond yield back to its ~2% long-term average; the yield curve inverted; discounted 10-year inflation stayed ~2% while the real yield rose to ~2%
criterion: TIPS real 10-yr ~2%, breakeven ~2%, curve inversion in 2023-24 data

claim: AI should greatly improve productivity and be disruptive; AI companies are the new hot thing expected to transform the economy like earlier revolutions that led to financial bubbles
criterion: Productivity data and whether an AI bubble forms and bursts

claim: Private credit is the modern version of the late-1970s/early-1980s junk bond market and has kept credit spreads down and funded more speculative activity
criterion: Spread levels and later default experience in private credit

claim: Trump's 2024 mandate includes renovating the central government and preparing for some type of war with China and its allies; a close Trump loss would likely have produced great conflict
criterion: Counterfactual plus intent; partly observable via defense posture

claim: The US domestic order/disorder cycle is at the same stage it was in the 1930s; the US-China conflict is intensifying; this looks quite like the 1930s period; it is the greatest great power conflict ever though not yet military
criterion: Only ex post (internal or external war)

claim: China is in a deleveraging that began in 2021 and is in the late part of the Big Debt Cycle most analogous to Japan in the 1990s; it has been slow to deal with it and it is unknown whether it will manage a beautiful deleveraging
criterion: Whether China restructures bad debt, holds rates below nominal growth, monetizes, and avoids prolonged deflation/stagnation

claim: China has moved about halfway back toward Maoist-Marxist communist policies
criterion: Judgment

claim: China's nominal government bond rates are approaching zero so non-conventional fiscal and monetary policies will likely have to be used; the yield curve was inverted as of late February 2025 and liquidity is rising without a real rebound (pushing on a string)
criterion: Adoption of QE/MP3-style policies by the PBoC/government; yield curve and TSF vs real activity

claim: China's real bond yield of ~0.5% is unattractive in a normal environment and relative to the US dollar bond market, though attractive vs a deflating economy
criterion: Relative real returns of CGBs vs Treasuries

claim: Chinese assets are now very cheap and non-debt-burdened innovative sectors will certainly be viable
criterion: Subsequent returns of Chinese equities and performance of those sectors

claim: If Japanese real rates rise 3% (from -0.3% to 2.7%): BoJ MTM loss ~30% of GDP and cash flow ~-2.5% of GDP; deficit 4% -> 8% of GDP over 10 years; debt 220% -> 300% over 20 years; combined need 5-6% of GDP per year; resolution requires bigger write-downs and devaluations
criterion: If JGB real yields rise ~3%: BoJ losses, deficit and debt paths

claim: Japan's debt service as a percent of revenue has risen toward but stayed below the 150% level at which past debt busts occurred
criterion: Debt service/revenue crossing 150% followed by a bust

claim: If rates rise, the BoJ will become significantly unprofitable fast; with a monetary base ~5x the Fed's its losses could be much more meaningful than the Fed's (~0.5% of GDP)
criterion: BoJ net income after a policy-rate rise

claim: Japanese equities' cheapening relative to other developed markets since 2013 has started to reverse in the past few years
criterion: Relative forward P/E of Japan vs peers

claim: Japan is preparing for war with China (though it does not want it) as the US's most important regional ally
criterion: Defense spending/posture only

claim: Rising neutral countries with strong fundamentals (India, Singapore, Indonesia, Vietnam, UAE, Saudi Arabia) are at take-off points, and the US-China conflict is driving capital, businesses and talent to them
criterion: Capital flows, FDI and growth in those countries

claim: The 1930s pattern (rightist governments squaring off against leftists, retreat from multilateralism, broken agreements, strongman unilateralism) is what we are now seeing in the US and several other countries
criterion: Analogy

claim: Germany is the one major country whose government debt/GDP is forecast to fall (to ~40% by 2050) in the Bloomberg Economics projection chart
criterion: German debt/GDP path

claim: US and post-1945 world order ~80 years into and ~90-95% through the Big Cycle; by his measures in Stage 5 of 6, on the brink of great conflicts and seismic shifts
criterion: Transition to Stage 6 (major conflict/order reset), observable only through his own stage classification

claim: US and other major economies ~5 years into and ~two-thirds through the 13th post-1945 short-term debt cycle; cycles run ~6 years give or take ~3
criterion: Onset of the next downturn that ends the cycle within the implied band

claim: Debt assets/liabilities piling up faster than income growth won't be sustained (good bet)
criterion: Debt-to-income growth stalls or reverses via restructuring, monetization or growth; no horizon given

claim: Conditions most analogous to 1905-14 and 1933-38; such times have always led to much more autocratic governance; all major powers are overindebted, inefficiently run and divided, producing nationalist, protectionist, militarist, autocratic leaders
criterion: Rise in autocracy indices and such policies across major powers

claim: If long-term Big Debt Cycle issues are not controlled, probability of an unwanted major restructuring/monetization of debt denominated in the major reserve currencies is 'something like 65% over the next five years and something like 80% over the next 10 years'
criterion: A major restructuring or monetization of USD/EUR/JPY government debt (large-scale QE or yield control to fund deficits, default, maturity extension) by those dates

claim: G7 total debt and debt service (% GDP) will rise to significantly higher levels, making it ever harder to set rates high enough for creditors without hurting debtors
criterion: G7 non-financial debt and debt service/GDP exceed current levels

claim: Next big red flag of an imminent debt crisis: significant selling of government bonds by existing holders, which with new issuance forces central banks to choose between much higher rates or printing to buy long bonds
criterion: Observed net selling by existing holders plus rising yields and central-bank intervention

claim: Extreme measures (freezing debt payments, seizing adversary assets, confiscatory taxes, capital/FX controls, defaults or maturity extensions, changing the type of money) are possible but 'more unlikely possibilities than high probabilities'
criterion: Any such measure enacted by a major reserve-currency government

claim: The era of borrowing far more than can be repaid to fund excess consumption is ending; goals shift to raising productivity and reducing the debt burden (which also reduces the value of debt and money)
criterion: Deficit reduction and/or real devaluation of debt; no horizon given

claim: Debt-service payments will keep rising to catch up with current interest rates because fixed-rate debt reprices with a lag
criterion: Government and private interest costs as % of GDP rise further

claim: Based on March 2025 inflation and growth readings, a Fed easing is not appropriate now; rates look about right by inflation/growth alone but are not high enough given the fiscal supply-demand dynamic
criterion: Policy judgment; testable only indirectly via subsequent inflation

claim: The Fed, effectively central banker to the world, will face much more criticism and interference; its independence should not be taken for granted
criterion: Erosion of Fed independence (links to red flag 2 on p. 333: government gaining control of the central bank)

claim: UK, France and some developing countries such as Brazil are already encountering government-debt supply-demand problems
criterion: Bond-market stress in those sovereigns

claim: Significant risk that both a debt squeeze and an economic downturn will happen simultaneously two or three years from now
criterion: US recession coinciding with government-bond demand/rollover stress in 2027-28

claim: The 'American exceptionalism' meme (AI, Trump/Musk efficiency) has merit but is now more than reflected in prices and there could be other big problems ahead
criterion: US risk assets underperform the expectations embedded in prices; no horizon given

claim: The too-much-debt problem will almost certainly lead to big fundamental changes in the monetary system, either pre-emptively or in response to the crisis; holding bonds becomes relatively undesirable versus storeholds of wealth that keep purchasing power
criterion: Structural change in monetary arrangements (new money type, hard-asset link, controls); bonds underperform real stores of value; no horizon

claim: Globalization is unstoppable and globalized deal-making is accelerating; financially strong, orderly, neutral emerging countries (India, Indonesia, ASEAN, GCC) will keep doing best while poor, disorderly, climate-hit countries fall further behind
criterion: Relative growth and capital flows of those country groups

claim: First-100-days honeymoon optimism gives way to disappointment, bolder critics, waning support and more extreme actions to hold power
criterion: Trajectory of presidential approval and escalation of executive actions

claim: Populist conflict between hard right, weak middle and hard left is producing big political shifts, mostly toward the hard right, and revolutionary changes; the least productive and poorest will suffer most
criterion: Election outcomes and policy direction across democracies; welfare of the bottom tiers

claim: Expect more fights between the executive and the other branches (especially the judiciary) and between federal, state and local governments; in a limits-of-power battle the judiciary will lose because the executive controls enforcement (DOJ, army, National Guard)
criterion: Executive non-compliance with or override of court rulings and the outcome of such standoffs

claim: 'We should expect many more power struggles. I have little doubt that the president will win most of these.'
criterion: Tally of executive-vs-institution confrontations won by the president

claim: Trump's 'make America great again' policies resemble those of hard-right countries in the 1930s; his bypassing of other branches is analogous to Andrew Jackson and FDR but more aggressive; aggressive leaders in great conflict work to eliminate opposition via threats, law changes granting special powers and media control, with laws and punishments targeting opponents if conflict becomes severe
criterion: Enactment of laws or punishments targeting the opposition; media control measures

claim: Radical government cuts will have negative second-order consequences (those hurt fight back; valuable support systems weakened); only a small share of the population is highly productive; check regularly on how the bottom 60% are doing
criterion: Measures of bottom-60% welfare and political backlash

claim: A type of world war is already under way, violent locally (Russia-Ukraine, Israel-Iran and proxies) but not yet between the US and China; the order is shifting from cooperative multilateral to confrontational unilateral
criterion: Escalation pattern of great-power conflict

claim: Europe is weak and easy prey; Russia will likely be an enemy of Europe; 'America First' will likely lead to the US not defending Europe
criterion: US withdrawal of security guarantees; Russian hostility toward Europe

claim: Alliances will change fast and in previously unimaginable ways: it would not surprise him if Trump's US and Putin's Russia align, isolating China, and if Europe and China become more aligned than Europe and the US
criterion: Observable US-Russia rapprochement; EU-China alignment exceeding EU-US alignment

claim: No US-China military war in the foreseeable future because of mutually assured destruction; China would fight only over a real threat to its sovereignty including Taiwan; no US president would fight unless facing an existential threat such as losing TSMC chip production
criterion: Absence of direct US-China military conflict

claim: Trump could be willing to negotiate Taiwan away under the right terms for a big price, provided any deal removes US semiconductor vulnerability; Taiwan should worry about being a bargaining chip
criterion: A US-China deal involving Taiwan's status

claim: The only way either side could win a war is by secretly building a technology of overwhelming power (atomic-bomb analogy); not ruled out because both are developing secret technologies
criterion: Demonstration of such a capability leading to capitulation

claim: His bet: China stays out of an overt fight for geopolitical dominance outside its region while building power to harm those who harm it and moving to unify Taiwan with China (a goal Xi, in his early 70s, wants in his lifetime); China keeps building Global South relationships
criterion: Chinese restraint outside its region; concrete moves toward Taiwan unification; Global South deals

claim: International investment and business deals will get easier and increase in number rather than get harder and fewer
criterion: Cross-border deal counts and volumes

claim: Acts of nature will increase in frequency and be very costly; little proactive prevention; climate displacement will strain the US and Europe via immigration and destabilize politics
criterion: Frequency and cost of natural disasters; migration pressures

claim: The technology force has never been more powerful; over the next five years we will see dramatic advancements in most areas as machine thinking supplements or surpasses human thinking
criterion: Broad AI-driven capability gains; 'dramatic' is not defined

claim: Exceptionally big performance differences between countries, investors and companies that use AI well and those that do not; unclear whether the money coming in will cover the cost of building these technologies
criterion: Dispersion of returns; AI capex versus revenue

claim: US leads in advanced chip design but is weak in production; China is close behind in advanced chips, ahead in cheap less-advanced chips and in deploying AI; IP protection does not work, so openly shown good ideas get replicated in about six months
criterion: Replication lag of frontier AI/chip advances

claim: Positive impacts of today's technologies will be about 150% of the past 30 years' digital boom, the most powerful technological revolution ever for markets and the economy, but most likely not enough to negate the headwinds of debt, internal conflict, external conflict, climate change and demographics; in prior episodes productivity gains were squelched when the other forces turned negative
criterion: Net real growth and market outcomes relative to the headwinds

claim: The next 5-10 years will be a period of enormous changes in all the major orders, like a time warp into a very different reality; many who are up will be down and vice versa
criterion: Regime changes in the monetary, domestic political and international orders; 'enormous' undefined

claim: Best places to be are countries that educate well, are civil, earn more than they spend, have internal order, low war risk, low nature risk and benefit from technology; human capital matters most
criterion: Relative performance of countries scoring well on those fundamentals (his Country Power Index)

claim: Objectively, the chances of cooperation for mutual benefit are not good: factions believe they must fight and win at all costs; extreme factionalism kills
criterion: Evidence of bipartisan/international cooperation versus escalation

claim: Changes in the orders will likely continue to track his template; he is at a maximum point of uncertainty 40 days into the new administration
criterion: Subsequent events match the Big Cycle sequence (self-referential)

claim: US government debt is nearing the point of no return (death-spiral threshold); short-term risk is 0% but can change overnight if demand for new/rolled debt falls or holders sell
criterion: Failed or weak auctions, net selling by holders, rate spike

claim: Fed long-term risk is small but could accelerate quickly; two red flags that should not happen but would signal great risk to the real value of money and debt: another round of QE forcing real rates down, and the central government gaining control over the central bank
criterion: QE resumption; loss of Fed independence

claim: He expects the president and Congress to pressure the Fed to lower interest rates
criterion: Public or formal pressure on the Fed to cut

claim: A significant enacted deficit reduction would trigger a rally in bonds and a decline in interest rates
criterion: Yields fall after major deficit-cut legislation

claim: If the 2017 Trump tax cuts are extended, the deficit will be larger by about 1.5% of GDP and the required cut rises to over 4% of GDP
criterion: CBO scoring of the extension

claim: Status quo (CBO assumptions): US government debt exceeds 130% of GDP in 20 years and reaches 7.2x revenue (from about 5.8x); 2035 projection 118% of GDP and 648% of revenue
criterion: Realized debt ratios versus projection

claim: If the plan is not implemented now, the debt problem grows and compounds (borrowing to service debt) and becomes more difficult to deal with
criterion: Debt and interest-to-revenue ratios rise absent a plan
